Abstract 
This paper outlines the technical and organizational measures implemented 
by the Italian supercomputing center, CINECA, to efficiently collect, process, and store 
sensitive-omics data in compliance with GDPR regulations. Indeed, the explosion 
of High Throughput Sequencing in medicine has raised tremendous opportunities 
for large-scale genomic data analysis. Cohort studies involving the processing of hun-
dreds or thousands of input samples, combined with the integration of diverse diag-
nostic data, enable researchers to conduct integrative analyses at an unprecedented 
level of detail would have been impossible to achieve through single sample studies. 
To analyse such amount of data, centres that have access to High Performance Com-
puting or extensive cloud resources have become crucial both for storage and efficient 
execution of data analysis pipelines. Nevertheless, since genomic data are consid-
ered sensitive personal data according to the EU General Data Protection Regulation, 
computational centres with high resource capabilities must prioritize data security 
and protection. This solution has been successfully applied to the Network for Ital-
ian Genomes use-case, demonstrating scalability to other hospitals and universities 
involved in research projects dealing with sensitive genomic data.

Introduction
Omics sciences refer to a plethora of biological disciplines whose names end in the suf-
fix ‘-omics’, such as genomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics, proteomics, epigenomics, 
radiomics and so on. This discipline has exploded thanks to the advent of High Through-
put Sequencing (HTS) experiments, which led to an explosion in the rate of data gener-
ated in recent years in the field of life science [36]. Processing large scale datasets like 
genomics data, presents significant tech challenges, making the use of High-Perfor-
mance Computing (HPC) infrastructures, which provide extensive computing resources 
and storage, nearly indispensable for handling such scale [18].

On the other hand, leveraging other computational resources which could poten-
tially raise many security and privacy concerns for individuals and healthcare provid-
ers [1]. In fact, starting from 2016, the European Commission adopted a General Data 
Protection Regulation (GDPR) which governs the processing of personal data of all EU 
citizens [44–51] raising concerns regarding the concepts of ‘personal data’ applied to 
genomics and what does the regulation means for researchers in healthcare. The GDPR 
classifies genetic data as “special categories of personal data” or sensitive data (Art. 9), 
meaning that their processing for research purposes (Art. 9(2)(j)) requires the imple-
mentation of appropriate organizational and technical safeguards, such as pseudonymi-
zation (Art. 89(1)) [25]. Pseudonymization is defined in Art. 4(5) as the process through 
which data “can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of 
additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and 
is subject to technical and organizational measures to ensure that the personal data are 
not attributed to an identified or identifiable natural person.” The GDPR defines pseu-
donymized data as personal data as well, thus falling within the scope of the regulation, 
and mandates that data be minimized and protected with appropriate security measures 
to prevent breaches. (Re-)identification is typically understood as either identity dis-
closure or attribute disclosure. Identity disclosure involves revealing a person’s identity, 
thereby compromising their anonymity, while attribute disclosure refers to the exposure 
of personal information, such as susceptibility to a disease, which constitutes a breach of 
privacy [8]. Since a number of studies demonstrated that 50 to 80 single nucleotide poly-
morphisms (SNPs) are sufficient to distinguish an individual’s DNA record [2, 19] even 
if the study reports only summary statistics such as allelic frequencies [16], the analysis 
of GDPR-protected data represents a great challenge when using shared and multi-user 
environments such as HPC facilities. This aspect greatly impacts clinical professionals, 
scientists, patients and data analysts [3].
For the above-mentioned reasons, the processing of identifiable data necessitates not 
only an appropriate legal basis, such as consent, but also the implementation of suffi-
cient organizational and technical safeguards. Aim of this paper is to present a platform 
that aims at providing a scalable, efficient, production-ready and secure environment 
for collecting, processing and storing sensitive “–omics” data. The adoption of this tech 
stack enabled CINECA to establish a work environment that fully adheres to informa-
tion security standards while simultaneously offering HPC services within its cloud 
infrastructure. This ensures that partners can manage their data in complete compliance 
with GDPR directives on personal data protection.
Case description
Technical implementation
Infrastructure
The schematic of the infrastructure shown in Fig. 1A comprises three virtual machines, 
each with a specific purpose, including a user interface server (VM1), a data aggregator 
(VM2) and a compute node (VM3). The user data and compute outputs are stored in 
an encrypted LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup) storage accessible to all three VMs. The 
workflow of the platform is the following: the researcher uploads the sequence data and 
the associated metadata via the application interface. The backend stores the metadata

in a dedicated database. The input data is processed with an analysis workflow imple-
mented using Snakemake (vide infra), and the computed outputs are stored in aggre-
gated form on the encrypted file system, which is then made available to the end user via 
the front-end.
Platform design
At a higher level, the individual components of the platform are deployed as Docker 
containers distributed across the VMs and orchestrated by the widely adopted Docker 
Swarm technology (Fig. 1B). In short, the Docker Swarm deploys the cluster as a Master-
Woker architecture. Here, the overall management of the cluster is hosted in one of the

VMs (master node), while the computational operations are performed in other VMs 
(worker nodes). This architecture ensures efficient scalability, as the cluster is extensible, 
with new workers added or removed according to computing demands.
Users can load samples and associated metadata via the frontend or directly by invok-
ing the underlying REST APIs. Access to the interface and APIs is granted via an https 
protocol using a client certificate in combination with Two-factor Authentication (2FA) 
protocol. A twelve-hour token is required to use the APIs and a new one is issued when 
user authentication reaches its maximum duration. Data are stored on a dedicated 
encrypted LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup) storage database.
The analysis pipeline runs in worker nodes with an instance of Celery, a framework 
widely used for distributed, asynchronous task execution. This helps to efficiently allo-
cate resources for the constant stream of incoming API requests and the ongoing exe-
cution of pipelines. Since the analysis of this type of data takes time and resources to 
complete, delegating the analysis to an asynchronous component can immediately set 
free the backend of the system which can promptly return available to manage further 
requests coming from the APIs and to manage additional functions. Instances of Celery 
running on different worker nodes are constantly monitored.
Since all VMs share the storage volume, output is stored on the same encrypted vol-
ume to which user data was previously uploaded, ensuring the privacy of processed files. 
The system periodically checks the availability of new records to analyse and, if so, sends 
a list of sample names via a message broker to the first available worker, which invokes 
the analysis pipeline. The task of message brokering is performed by the Redis compo-
nent, which delivers the message to an asynchronous task queue based on Celery. The 
choice to manage analysis operations through an asynchronous task queue addresses 
two needs: scalability and resource management efficiency.
Security measures
In accordance with GDPR, which has become effective on May 25th, 2018, and consider-
ing the additional measures imposed by Italy, genetic data are classified as “special cat-
egories of personal data” (Art. 9). According to Recital 51: “Personal data which are, by 
their nature, particularly sensitive in relation to fundamental rights and freedoms merit 
specific protection as the context of their processing could create significant risks to the 
fundamental rights and freedoms.” Therefore, when processing genetic data for research 
or clinical purposes, it is mandatory to adopt adequate privacy safeguards. The GDPR 
mandates a decentralized and risk-based approach to data protection with emphasis on 
the accountability of data controllers to structure a flexible governance for data protec-
tion [25]. Additionally, the processing of personal data for scientific research falls into 
the field of a so-called “research exemption”, where the GDPR allows for some flexibility 
(Art. 9(2)(j)), such as data anonymization [34] and it relaxes the stringent requirements 
for data storage (Art. 5 (1)(e)) and specific consent (Recital 33).
The technical safeguards adopted by CINECA, and described within this article, 
ensure that personal and sensitive data can be managed in compliance with current law.
The following three examples can help explain how the adopted security measures can 
protect data.

1.	 Volume encryption helps ensure compliance with GDPR regulations by providing 
robust protection against unauthorized access. In fact, only the users with authoriza-
tion to login into the virtual machine will view the data in its "in clear" (decrypted) 
form. This approach combines volume encryption with access control mechanisms 
to ensure that sensitive data is protected both at rest and during access.
2.	 Data access controls: Access to sensitive data is strictly controlled through role-based 
access controls (RBAC). Only authorized personnel have access to specific subsets of 
the data necessary for their roles. By limiting data access to authorized users only, the 
risk of unauthorized access is minimized, ensuring that personal health information 
remains secure.
3.	 Regular Security Audits and Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs): Regular 
audits and DPIAs help to proactively identify and mitigate risks, thereby preventing 
data breaches and ensuring continuous compliance with data protection laws.
Table 1 summarizes the implemented privacy-preserving measures, divided by macro 
area: Data collection, system architecture, data access, bureaucratic and data breach 
prevention.
Overall, the above-mentioned five macro-areas, provide a comprehensive framework 
that aligns well with the overall workflow of data protection for the management of sen-
sitive and personal data in the field of life sciences. Taken together, these security meas-
ures allowed CINECA to gain both the ISO 9001 (Quality Management Systems) and 
ISO/IEC 27001 (Information Security Management Systems) certifications in this area.
NIG use‑case
To demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed solution, an HPC and GDPR-compliant 
platform architecture has been deployed on a real use case, the NIG (Network for Italian 
Genomes), a consortium composed by nine Italian hospitals and research centers. NIG 
project aims at creating a a catalogue of human genome variants referred to the Italian 
population derived from clinical exomes., particularly Single Nucleotide Polimorphisms 
(SNPs) and Insertions/Deletions (InDELs) observed by analyzing samples derived from 
HTS experiments over thousands of human samples. The main challenge of this project 
is data aggregation to obtain a repository enabling users to:
•	 Identify genes responsible for genetic diseases and susceptibility genes for complex 
diseases in both basic and translational researchers.
•	 Discover new genetic variants responsible for interindividual differences in drug 
response in the Italian population or variants useful for forensic purposes.
•	 Highlight new targets for diagnosing and treating genetic diseases.
To obtain the reference genome of the Italian population the input samples need to 
be merged together to increase the statistical significance of the results but, at the same 
time, it is mandatory to preserve data privacy from individual samples.
Such input data is uploaded by each NIG-affiliated member whose access is strictly 
limited to those possessing a valid digital certificate to be installed on the client-side. 
Data upload follows quality and regulatory requirements already in place to ensure

Workflow management system
One of the challenges of the use-case here described was to create an optimal workflow 
for analysing a large cohort of human exomes. In fact, when the amounts of raw data 
produced are immense, many computational steps are required to translate this output 
into high-quality variant calls [6] and some crucial steps such as debugging and work-
flow resuming can be nearly impossible when thousands of samples undergo in com-
plex workflows run in parallel. Therefore, we adopted a unified analytic framework to 
discover and genotype variations among thousands of samples simultaneously. Work-
flow engines such as Snakemake [28] help to automate these pipelines and ensure repro-
ducibility [15], moreover they can automatically determine which parts of the workflow 
can be run in parallel and help optimizing the whole stream of analysis. Furthermore, 
since new datasets are continuously injected into the stream, Snakemake has the cru-
cial feature of recognizing which samples have already been analysed, thus enabling the 
processing of newly added samples only. Once data have been uploaded, the workers 
launch jobs through the WMS and dispatch the analyses over the 96 vCPUs available on 
each VM. The Celery component takes over the analysis task and invokes an instance 
of Snakemake to run it. On the other hand, Snakemake takes care of orchestrating the 
available resources between the different tasks to optimize their use and analysis times.
For what concerns the technical details of the bioinformatics analysis (Fig. 2), each 
sample is genotyped and the VCF (variant calling format) output files are stored in the 
encrypted volume.
After single sample analysis is complete, a joint-variant calling analysis step is exe-
cuted, thus enormously empowering variant discovery by providing the ability to lever-
age population-wide information from a cohort of multiple samples. This step detects 
variants with great sensitivity and genotypes samples as accurately as possible produc-
ing a call set in VCF format [40]. Once variants are called, it is crucial to recognize the

Error check
Given the large number of samples and the potential for the pipeline to misbehave at 
various random steps due to unexpected errors that don’t necessarily stop its over-
all execution, it’s crucial for the pipeline to detect and handle these issues. Addition-
ally, the pipeline should be able to resume from where it left off without recomputing 
completed steps, thereby saving valuable time and computational resources. Fortu-
nately, most WMS generate a large set of logs for each of the jobs executed allowing 
maintainers to identify any possible issues. However, the sheer volume of samples and 
jobs makes it nearly impossible to review each log individually, impacting the scalabil-
ity of the workload.
To address this challenge, we developed a suite of log-checker python scripts able to 
collect the signatures released by each step of the analysis to track job status, control 
the flow progression of data processing and parse execution information such as file 
locations and input/output information.
Two strategies were followed to verify that a run executed without any unexpected 
errors:
•	 Baseline Log Comparison: This approach assumes that the logs of incorrect runs 
differ in meaningful ways from those in which the runs encountered and unex-
pected error. We identified a set of relevant markers from such logs, and whenever 
we recorded a difference with respect to the current run, an alert was highlighted 
to analyse in more detail. Examples of such markers are the number of rows gen-
erated by some of the logs, the consistency of values from one log to another, that 
the location of where logs were searching for data was the expected one, etc. On 
average we implemented 8 tests for each of the steps in the pipeline tailored on the 
type of logs each of these generate. Despite its simplicity, this method has allowed 
us to identify multiple misbehaviours, most of which were caused to the quality of 
the samples uploaded, leading to anomalous logs.
•	 Anomaly Detection: A more robust approach was tested in which several fea-
tures were extracted from each log output. Starting from the “correct” expected 
log files, we were able to create a distribution function of such features, giving 
us the most likely behaviour. Whenever a feature from a new run would fall out-
side of this distribution function an alert would be generated. This approach falls 
inside an active learning paradigm given that the distribution function is updated 
every time a “correct” run is verified. More data is being collected to make sure 
this method provides reliable results (which would otherwise generate large num-
ber of irrelevant false positives) before being deployed in production.
When an unexpected error is identified using either strategy, an alert is generated 
and sent to the system administrator. Since some of these errors might be false posi-
tives, the pipeline continues running, but the alert highlights the exact point where

error needs to be addressed or can be safely ignored.
Platform scalability and performance
Data has been analyzed using 2 VMs equipped with 96 CPUs and benchmarks were 
computed over a subset of 200 samples ranging from 3 to 23 GB in input size each. The 
average time for Snakemake to complete a run was 8 h per-sample. Since Snakemake 
can dispatch the samples over all the available vCPUs on the VM and considering that 
the most demanding rule in terms of threads is read mapping (16 vCPUs per-sample), 
this means that up to 6 samples can be analyzed in parallel over a single VM during the 
mapping process. Conversely, when other rules requiring at most 2 vCPUS are executed 
(e.g., HaplotypeCaller or BQSR), up to 24 samples can be analyzed in parallel, making 
the most of all the resources that become available. Therefore, considering several vari-
ables such as sample size, number of available VMs and processing steps with hetero-
geneous requirements in terms of threads, we have been able to process an average of 
175 samples per week using 2 VMs. This number can be easily adjusted upon needs, by 
simply adding new workers to the system, thus ensuring data processing scalability over 
hundreds or thousands of samples (Fig. 4).

Cloud HPC CINECA infrastructure
The Cloud Computing IaaS infrastructure, named “ADA Cloud” in memory of the math-
ematician Ada Lovelace, is based on OpenStack Wallaby release and was first installed

The storage, directly connected and fully dedicated to OpenStack, is made of 12 serv-
ers equipped with 1 PB of total raw disks. The storage is full flash NVMe/SSD, managed

form open-source) is configured for providing both block-storage and File System stor-
age services. To address high performance computing, no oversubscription of resources 
is allowed (Fig. 5).
The OpenStack installation on the physical servers was done using the Kolla-Ansible 
system, based on Ubuntu 20.4, configured for the installation of the core services both 
on the Cloud Controller and Compute Nodes with the QEMU-KVM hypervisor. Both 
software and hardware architectures are implemented fully redundant, to avoid Single 
Point of Failure (SPoF) events.
Even if the cloud part is isolated from the scalable part of GALILEO100, some interac-
tions can be set up for selected use cases. The goal GALILEO100 was built for is to pro-
vide the user with a general-purpose environment. The hardware used to build it aims 
for maximum performance while allowing to address complex user workflows involving 
flexible user environments and traditional HPC simulations. Moreover, the cloud HPC 
infrastructure is tightly connected both to the GALILEO100 LUSTRE storage of 20 PB

Discussion and evaluation
Genome sequencing projects are uncovering millions of genetic variants in living 
organisms and interpreting their functional effects is essential for understanding the 
genetic basis of variation in human traits. Nevertheless, the advent of the GDPR has 
provided European and Italian legislators with the opportunity to establish a robust 
privacy framework, ensuring the protection of sensitive genomic data [3]. Since the 
GDPR gives to Member States the opportunity to implement additional limitations 


Page 13 of 16
Gioiosa et al. Journal of Big Data           (2025) 12:31 
	
on specific data processing, Italy took advantage of this provision, tasking the DPA 
with defining special conditions for handling health and genetic data [31]. The unique 
nature of genetic data, which reveals information about not only the individual but 
also their relatives, underscores the need for stringent privacy safeguards [5].
For these reasons, the analysis of GDPR-protected data represents a non-trivial 
challenge when using shared and multi-user environments such as HPC facilities, 
which in turn become mandatory when dealing with big data. In this scenario, cloud-
based infrastructures designed with the necessary security measures to meet privacy 
standards are becoming increasingly popular for hosting platforms used in scientific 
and medical applications [14]. These architectures offer scalability and secure data 
storage, making them suitable for large-scale collaborative research projects, such as 
the curated databases of common and rare genetic variants such as the 1000 Genome 
Project Consortium [17, 37]. This is exemplified by consortia like the Network for Ital-
ian Genomes (NIG), aimed at creating the Italian Reference Genome database. NIG 
enables clinicians and researchers to contribute WES data from various hospitals, 
enhancing the ability to interpret genetic variation. As the database grows, the archi-
tecture can be scaled by adding more virtual VMs, maintaining processing capacity to 
accommodate the ever-increasing data load.
This continuous injection of data is a critical milestone for improving the accuracy of 
variant frequency estimates within the Italian population. Ensuring GDPR compliance 
was a primary focus, making this one of the first successful implementations of such a 
secure, compliant platform in Italy. The use of a Workflow Management System (WMS) 
has further enhanced data governance, ensuring reproducibility and automation as the 
dataset grows. Moreover, Snakemake’s scalability and flexibility is also optimal and tai-
lored to ’-omics’ data, which typically involves many big-sized samples. In the end, an 
automatic log checking system has been implemented to take actions to remedy any 
undetected bugs that may occur during data processing.
The bioinformatics architecture developed for NIG was designed to be as general-
purpose as possible, meaning that CINECA’s cloud-secure, GDPR-compliant HPC 
environment can accommodate diverse research needs, including transcriptomics, 
metagenomics, radiomics and other types of analyses.
Conclusions
The successful deployment of an HPC cloud platform for genomic analysis has broad 
implications for both personalized medicine and collaborative research. The secure, scal-
able infrastructure described in this paper enables researchers across different hospitals 
to leverage high-performance computing and advanced bioinformatics tools to analyse 
large datasets efficiently. This supports more effective disease research, drug develop-
ment, and clinical decision-making, thereby advancing the field of personalized medi-
cine. As genomic data production grows, the need for more efficient processing, storage, 
and analysis methods becomes increasingly important. Such flexibility is crucial given 
the rapid expansion of genomic data, which is doubling every 18 months [18]. There are 
several promising areas for future exploration. First, the continued development of more 
sophisticated data pipelines for different types of genomic and biomedical data, such as 
metagenomics and transcriptomics, will be essential. Second, the integration of more

tions [29]. We are currently experimenting with NVIDIA Clara Parabricks containers 
on 2 cloud nodes equipped with 4 A100 GPUs and our future perspectives will be equip-

in minutes. In fact, our first tests on human Whole Genome Sequencing samples con-

remains a critical area for further research in national and international cooperation.

Abstract: This paper outlines the technical and organizational measures implemented by the Italian supercomputing center, CINECA, to efficiently collect, process, and store sensitive-omics data in compliance with GDPR regulations. Indeed, the explosion of High Throughput Sequencing in medicine has raised tremendous opportunities for large-scale genomic data analysis. Cohort studies involving the processing of hun- dreds or thousands of input samples, combined with the integration of diverse diag- nostic data, enable researchers to conduct integrative analyses at an unprecedented level of detail would have been impossible to achieve through single sample studies. To analyse such amount of data, centres that have access to High Performance Com- puting or extensive cloud resources have become crucial both for storage and efficient execution of data analysis pipelines. Nevertheless, since genomic data are consid- ered sensitive personal data according to the EU General Data Protection Regulation, computational centres with high resource capabilities must prioritize data security and protection. This solution has been successfully applied to the Network for Ital- ian Genomes use-case, demonstrating scalability to other hospitals and universities involved in research projects dealing with sensitive genomic data.
